[[File:Ookunitamajinjya.ootorii.jpg|thumb|The Great Torii and shrine name pillar]]
{{nihongo|'''Ōkunitama Shrine'''|大國魂神社}} is a {{ill|Shinto shrine|abstract|Q845945|ar|جينجا|arz|ضريح شنتو|bcl|Shinto shrine|ca|Jinja|cs|Šintoistická svatyně|da|Shinto-tempel|de|Shintō-Schrein|el|Σιντοϊστικό Ιερό|eo|Ŝintoa sanktejo|es|Jinja|eu|Jinja|fa|معبد شینتویی|fi|Šintolainen pyhäkkö|fr|Sanctuaire shinto|hi|शिंतो मंदिर|hr|Šintoistički hram|hu|Sintó szentély|id|Jinja|it|Jinja|ja|神社|ka|ძინძია|ko|신사 (신토)|lb|Shintō-Schräin|mr|शिंतो मंदिर|nl|Jinja (heiligdom)|no|Jinja|or|ଜିଞ୍ଜା|pl|Jinja|pt|Templo xintoísta|ru|Дзиндзя|sc|Jinja|simple|Shinto shrine|sl|Šintoistično svetišče|sr|Шинтоистички храм|sv|Jinja|th|ศาลเจ้าชินโต|tok|tomo sewi pi nasin sewi Sinto|tr|Şinto tapınağı|uk|Святилище (синто)|uz|Dzindzya|vi|Thần xã|wuu|神社|zh|神社|zh_yue|神社|qid=Q845945|lt=Shinto shrine}} located in {{ill|Tokyo|Q1490|qid=Q1490|lt=Tokyo Metropolis}}, {{ill|Fuchū, Tokyo|Q208818|qid=Q208818|lt=Fuchū City}}, {{ill|Miyamachi|Q116980587|qid=Q116980587|lt=Miyamachi}}. It is the {{ill|Sōja shrine|Q1107129|qid=Q1107129|lt=sōja}} (provincial shrine) of {{ill|Musashi Province|Q907398|qid=Q907398|lt=Musashi Province}} and one of the Tokyo Five Shrines.<ref group="注">The other four are {{ill|Tokyo Daijingu|Q11524717|qid=Q11524717|lt=Tokyo Daijingu}}, {{ill|Yasukuni Shrine|Q242803|qid=Q242803|lt=Yasukuni Shrine}}, {{ill|Hie Shrine|Q702042|qid=Q702042|lt=Hie Shrine}}, and {{ill|Meiji Shrine|Q287165|qid=Q287165|lt=Meiji Shrine}}.</ref> Because it enshrines together the deities from the First through Sixth Shrines of Musashi Province, it is also known as '''Rokushō-gū''' (“Shrine of Six Deities”). {{nihongo|'''Ōkunitama Shrine'''|大國魂神社}} is a [[shinto shrine]] in the [[Engishiki Jinmyōchō]]. It is located in [[Musashi Province]].

== Overview ==
[[File:Musashi.kokufu.ato.fuchu.tokyo.jpg|thumb|Historic Site: {{ill|Musashi Kokufu|Q11546339|qid=Q11546339|lt=Ruins of the Musashi Provincial Capital}}]]
[[File:Furusato.fuchu.rekishikan.jpg|thumb|Furusato Fuchū History Museum]]
In {{ill|Ancient history|Q41493|qid=Q41493|lt=ancient times}}, {{ill|Kokushi (official)|Q1351234|qid=Q1351234|lt=provincial governors}} visited all the shrines in their jurisdiction, starting from the ichinomiya (first shrine). To simplify this long pilgrimage, a {{ill|Sōja shrine|Q1107129|qid=Q1107129|lt=sōja}} was established near each province’s {{ill|Kokufu|Q1629088|qid=Q1629088|lt=provincial capital}}, where the gods of the province were collectively enshrined. This shrine served as the sōja of {{ill|Musashi Province|Q907398|qid=Q907398|lt=Musashi Province}}.

The shrine stands in the center of Fuchū City; the city name “Fuchū” derives from the former location of the Musashi provincial capital. The shrine grounds occupy the site of that capital, while the municipal land to the east across the road is designated a national {{ill|Historic site|ar|الموقع التاريخي|azb|تاریخی مکان|bn|ঐতিহাসিক স্থান|es|Patrimonio histórico|fa|بنای تاریخی|fr|Site historique|hy|Պատմության հուշարձան|id|Situs bersejarah|ja|史跡|ka|ისტორიული ძეგლი|ko|사적|pt|Patrimônio histórico|ru|Исторический памятник|sq|Vende historike|ta|வரலாற்று இடம்|tr|Tarihî mekân|uk|Пам'ятка історії|zh|古蹟|zh_min_nan|Kó͘-chek|qid=Q1081138|lt=historic site}} as the “{{ill|Musashi Kokufu|Q11546339|qid=Q11546339|lt=Musashi Provincial Capital Ruins}} (Musashi Government Office Area).” This eastern area has been developed with marked pillar sites and exhibition rooms, and includes the Furusato Fuchū History Museum. The shrine is also near the center of {{ill|Fuchū Post Town|Q11486027|qid=Q11486027|lt=Fuchū Post Town}}, and a road once connected the Great Torii to {{ill|Musashi Kokubun-ji Remains|Q11546338|qid=Q11546338|lt=Musashi Kokubunji}} and the Musashi {{ill|provincial nunnery|Q131908135|qid=Q131908135|lt=Kokubunniji}}.

According to tradition, the shrine was founded on May 5, 111 CE, in the 41st year of {{ill|Emperor Keikō|Q329723|qid=Q329723|lt=Emperor Keikō}}, and the provincial capital was established here during the {{ill|Taika Reform|Q570140|qid=Q570140|lt=Taika Reforms}}. Legends recount that {{ill|Minamoto no Yoriyoshi|Q3082851|qid=Q3082851|lt=Minamoto no Yoriyoshi}} and {{ill|Minamoto no Yoshiie|Q32613|qid=Q32613|lt=Minamoto no Yoshiie}} prayed here for victory before campaigns in {{ill|Mutsu Province|Q907389|qid=Q907389|lt=Mutsu Province}}, and that their descendant {{ill|Minamoto no Yoritomo|Q242800|qid=Q242800|lt=Minamoto no Yoritomo}} prayed for the safe childbirth of his {{ill|Wife|Q188830|qid=Q188830|lt=wife}}.

The grounds contain many shrine buildings and numerous cultural properties, including wooden {{ill|Komainu|Q20155846|qid=Q20155846|lt=komainu}} designated as {{ill|Important Cultural Property (Japan)|Q1188622|qid=Q1188622|lt=Important Cultural Properties}}. Despite its location in the city center near {{ill|Fuchūhommachi Station|Q800794|qid=Q800794|lt=Fuchū-Hommachi Station}}, the shrine is surrounded by trees, and the {{ill|Babadaimon no Keyaki Namiki|Q11667865|qid=Q11667865|lt=Baba-Daimon Zelkova Avenue}} along the approach is designated a national Natural Monument.

The shrine’s main festival is the '''{{ill|Kurayami Matsuri|Q11265601|qid=Q11265601|lt=Kurayami Festival}}''', designated a {{ill|Tokyo Metropolitan Intangible Folk Cultural Property|Q11525325|qid=Q11525325|lt=Tokyo Metropolitan Intangible Folk Cultural Property}} and counted among the three great “strange festivals” of the {{ill|Kantō|Q11655841|qid=Q11655841|lt=Kantō}} region.

== Enshrined Deities ==
The main hall enshrines the following deities. As the sōja of Musashi Province, it enshrines together the deities of the First through Sixth Shrines of Musashi (collectively known as the Bushū Rokusha Myōjin).
; Central Hall
* '''Ōkunitama Ōkami''' – Principal deity; identified with {{ill|UNKNOWN|lt=大国主神}}.
* Goryō Ōkami
* Deities of the Province
; Eastern Hall
* First Shrine: Ono Ōkami – {{ill|Ono Shrine|Q11464224|qid=Q11464224|lt=Ono Shrine}} ({{ill|Tama, Tokyo|Q213263|qid=Q213263|lt=Tama City}}, Tokyo)
* Second Shrine: Ogawa Ōkami – {{ill|Ninomiya Shrine|Q11371508|qid=Q11371508|lt=Ninomiya Shrine}} ({{ill|Akiruno, Tokyo|Q240480|qid=Q240480|lt=Akiruno City}}, Tokyo)<ref name=ninomiya group="注">Although this shrine enshrines Ninomiya Shrine as the second shrine at the time of its founding, historically there is also a theory that {{ill|Kanasana Shrine|Q11647974|qid=Q11647974|lt=Kanayama Shrine}} was the second shrine.</ref>
* Third Shrine: Hikawa Ōkami – {{ill|Hikawa Shrine (Saitama)|Q703633|qid=Q703633|lt=Hikawa Shrine}} ({{ill|Saitama Prefecture|Q128186|qid=Q128186|lt=Saitama Prefecture}}, {{ill|Saitama (city)|Q134635|qid=Q134635|lt=Saitama City}}, {{ill|Ōmiya-ku, Saitama|Q153629|qid=Q153629|lt=Ōmiya Ward}})
; Western Hall
* Fourth Shrine: Chichibu Ōkami – {{ill|Chichibu Shrine|Q2963366|qid=Q2963366|lt=Chichibu Shrine}} ({{ill|Chichibu, Saitama|Q647079|qid=Q647079|lt=Chichibu City}}, Saitama)
* Fifth Shrine: Kanasa Ōkami – {{ill|Kanasana Shrine|Q11647974|qid=Q11647974|lt=Kanayama Shrine}} ({{ill|Kodama District, Saitama|Q938038|qid=Q938038|lt=Kodama District}}, {{ill|Kamikawa, Saitama|Q1346757|qid=Q1346757|lt=Kamikawa Town}}, Saitama)<ref name=ninomiya group="注"/>
* Sixth Shrine: Sugiyama Ōkami – {{ill|Sugiyama Shrine|Q11521945|qid=Q11521945|lt=Sugiyama Shrine}} ({{ill|Kanagawa Prefecture|Q127513|qid=Q127513|lt=Kanagawa Prefecture}}, {{ill|Yokohama|Q38283|qid=Q38283|lt=Yokohama}}, {{ill|Midori-ku, Yokohama|Q1203373|qid=Q1203373|lt=Midori Ward}})<ref group="注">Multiple shrines claim to be the Sixth Shrine of Musashi.</ref>

It is said that in the early years, Shinto priests from across Musashi gathered on the founding date, May 5, to perform prayers.

== History ==
[[File:Edomeisyozue.v2.p346.jpg|thumb|{{ill|Edo meisho zue|Q2704637|qid=Q2704637|lt=Illustrated Famous Places of Edo}}: Fuchū Rokushō-gū]]

== Founding ==
According to shrine traditions such as the *Fuchū Rokushō-sha Den*, Ōkunitama Ōkami descended to this place on May 5 in the 41st year of {{ill|Emperor Keikō|Q329723|qid=Q329723|lt=Emperor Keikō}}, and the local people enshrined him. Descendants of {{ill|UNKNOWN|lt=天穂日命}}, ancestral deity of the {{ill|UNKNOWN|lt=出雲氏}}, were appointed as {{ill|UNKNOWN|lt=武蔵国造}} and served the shrine for generations.

The founding of the shrine is traditionally said to date to the 41st year of Emperor Keikō (May 5, 111 CE), and it is said that during the {{ill|Taika Reform|Q570140|qid=Q570140}} the provincial government was placed at its present location. Traditions remain that {{ill|Minamoto no Yoriyoshi|Q3082851|qid=Q3082851}} and {{ill|Minamoto no Yoshiie|Q32613|qid=Q32613|lt=Yoshiie}} prayed here for victory when heading to the wars in {{ill|Mutsu Province|Q907389|qid=Q907389|lt=Ōshū}}, and that their direct descendant {{ill|Minamoto no Yoritomo|Q242800|qid=Q242800}} also prayed here for the safe childbirth of his {{ill|Wife|Q188830|qid=Q188830}}.

The precincts consist of many shrine buildings and preserve numerous cultural properties, including wooden {{ill|Komainu|Q20155846|qid=Q20155846}} designated as {{ill|Important Cultural Property (Japan)|Q1188622|qid=Q1188622}}. Although it is located in the center of the city near {{ill|Fuchūhommachi Station|Q800794|qid=Q800794}}, it is surrounded by trees, and the approach lined with zelkova trees known as {{ill|Babadaimon no Keyaki Namiki|Q11667865|qid=Q11667865}} is designated a National Natural Monument.

The shrine’s {{ill|UNKNOWN|lt=例大祭}} is the “'''{{ill|Kurayami Matsuri|Q11265601|qid=Q11265601}}''',” which is designated as a {{ill|Tokyo Metropolitan Intangible Folk Cultural Property|Q11525325|qid=Q11525325|lt=Tokyo Metropolitan Intangible Folk Cultural Property}} and is counted as one of the three great {{ill|kisai|Q11444891|qid=Q11444891}} of the {{ill|Kantō|Q11655841|qid=Q11655841}} region. 

== Enshrined Deities ==
The deities enshrined in the main hall are as follows. As the general shrine of Musashi Province, it enshrines the deities of the First through Sixth Shrines of Musashi Province at the time of its founding (commonly called the Six Shrines of Bushū).
; Central Hall
* '''Ōkunitama Ōkami''' (おおくにたまのおおかみ) – Principal deity. Considered identical to {{ill|UNKNOWN|lt=大国主神}}.
* Goryō Ōkami
* Deities of the Province
; Eastern Hall
* First Shrine: Ono Ōkami – {{ill|Ono Shrine|Q11464224|qid=Q11464224|lt=Ono Shrine}} ({{ill|Tama, Tokyo|Q213263|qid=Q213263}}, Tokyo)
* Second Shrine: Ogawa Ōkami – {{ill|Ninomiya Shrine|Q11371508|qid=Q11371508|lt=Ninomiya Shrine}} ({{ill|Akiruno, Tokyo|Q240480|qid=Q240480}}, Tokyo)<ref name=ninomiya group="注">At this shrine, Ninomiya Shrine is enshrined as the Second Shrine at the time of the founding; however, historically there is also a theory that the Fifth Shrine, Kanzan Shrine, was considered the Second Shrine (see “{{ill|Ichinomiya|Q1656379|qid=Q1656379}}”).</ref>
* Third Shrine: Hikawa Ōkami – {{ill|Hikawa Shrine (Saitama)|Q703633|qid=Q703633}} ({{ill|Saitama Prefecture|Q128186|qid=Q128186}}{{ill|Saitama (city)|Q134635|qid=Q134635}}{{ill|Ōmiya-ku, Saitama|Q153629|qid=Q153629}})
; Western Hall
* Fourth Shrine: Chichibu Ōkami – {{ill|Chichibu Shrine|Q2963366|qid=Q2963366}} ({{ill|Chichibu, Saitama|Q647079|qid=Q647079}}, Saitama Prefecture)
* Fifth Shrine: Kanasa Ōkami – {{ill|Kanasana Shrine|Q11647974|qid=Q11647974}} ({{ill|Kodama District, Saitama|Q938038|qid=Q938038}}{{ill|Kamikawa, Saitama|Q1346757|qid=Q1346757}}, Saitama Prefecture)<ref name=ninomiya group="注"/>
* Sixth Shrine: Sugiyama Ōkami – {{ill|Sugiyama Shrine|Q11521945|qid=Q11521945|lt=Sugiyama Shrine}} ({{ill|Kanagawa Prefecture|Q127513|qid=Q127513}}{{ill|Yokohama|Q38283|qid=Q38283}}{{ill|Midori-ku, Yokohama|Q1203373|qid=Q1203373|lt=Midori Ward}})<ref group="注">This shrine regards the Sugiyama Shrine in Nishihassaku-chō, Midori Ward, as the Sixth Shrine, but there are multiple claimant shrines for the Sixth Shrine of Musashi Province (see “{{ill|Sukiyamano Shrine|Q135039726|qid=Q135039726}}”).</ref>

In the early period after its establishment, it is said that on the founding date of May 5, priests from all over Musashi Province gathered to perform prayers.

== History ==
[[File:Edomeisyozue.v2.p346.jpg|thumb|{{ill|Edo meisho zue|Q2704637|qid=Q2704637}} Fuchū Rokusho Shrine]]

== Founding ==
According to traditions recorded in shrine records such as *Fuchū Rokusho Shrine Tradition*, Ōkunitama Ōkami descended to this place on May 5 in the 41st year of Emperor Keikō, and the local people enshrined the deity, forming the origin of the shrine. Thereafter, descendants of {{ill|UNKNOWN|lt=天穂日命}}, the ancestral deity of the {{ill|UNKNOWN|lt=Izumo clan}}, were appointed as {{ill|UNKNOWN|lt=武蔵国造}} and served the shrine; successive provincial rulers performed the rites and administration of worship<ref>{{cite book|和書| author=Tokyo Prefecture (ed.)| title=Tokyo Prefecture Nishitama District, Minamitama District, Kitatama District Guide to Famous Places, Historic Sites, and Products| chapter=Ōkunitama Shrine| year=1912| publisher=Tokyo Prefecture| pages=pp. 92f| url={{NDLDC|946884/117}}}}</ref>. At that time, the shrine was called “Ōkunitama Shrine.”

== Overview ==
* {{ill|Taika (era)|Q1077930|qid=Q1077930}} 1 ({{ill|645|Q31040|qid=Q31040}}) – During the {{ill|Taika Reform|Q570140|qid=Q570140}}, the provincial capital of Musashi was placed within the precincts, and the shrine became the ritual site of the provincial government, with the governor overseeing the rites of the province. Deities of the province were enshrined for the convenience of offerings and rituals, forming the origin of the Musashi General Shrine. At this time, the name became “Musashi General Shrine,” and later, with the enshrinement of six notable deities of Musashi Province, it became “Musashi General Shrine Rokusho-no-miya.”
* {{ill|Kōhei|Q1193572|qid=Q1193572}} 5 (1062) – During the pacification of the {{ill|Former Nine Years' War|Q1187448|qid=Q1187448}}, {{ill|Minamoto no Yoriyoshi|Q3082851|qid=Q3082851}} and {{ill|Minamoto no Yoshiie|Q32613|qid=Q32613|lt=Yoshiie}} donated one thousand saplings of {{ill|Zelkova serrata|Q920344|qid=Q920344|lt=zelkova}}. This became the origin of the present {{ill|Babadaimon no Keyaki Namiki|Q11667865|qid=Q11667865}}, now a National {{ill|Natural monument|Q23790|qid=Q23790}}. Also, because {{ill|Prunus salicina|Q1250033|qid=Q1250033|lt=plums}} were offered as {{ill|Sacred food as offering|Q12682000|qid=Q12682000}}, the annual “Plum Festival” came to be held on {{ill|July 20|Q2728|qid=Q2728}}.
* {{ill|Juei|Q598057|qid=Q598057}} 1 (1182) – {{ill|Minamoto no Yoritomo|Q242800|qid=Q242800}} sent {{ill|Kasai Kiyoshige|Q11621006|qid=Q11621006|lt=Kassai Saburō Kiyoshige}} as an envoy to pray for the safe childbirth of {{ill|Hōjō Masako|Q463961|qid=Q463961|lt=Masako}}.
* {{ill|Bunji (era)|Q1194415|qid=Q1194415}} 2 (1186) – Yoritomo appointed {{ill|Hiraga Yoshinobu|Q11483573|qid=Q11483573|lt=Hiraga Yoshinobu}} as {{ill|Bugyō|Q2535820|qid=Q2535820}} to construct shrine buildings.
* {{ill|Jōei|Q1194168|qid=Q1194168}} 1, 2nd month (1232) – Repairs were carried out under {{ill|Hōjō Yasutoki|Q1188359|qid=Q1188359}}, the third {{ill|Shikken|Q1045904|qid=Q1045904}} of the {{ill|Kamakura shogunate|Q736839|qid=Q736839}}.
* {{ill|Tenshō (Momoyama period)|Q1145058|qid=Q1145058}} 18 (1590), 8th month – After {{ill|Tokugawa Ieyasu|Q171977|qid=Q171977}} entered Edo, 500 koku of shrine lands were donated as the general shrine of Musashi Province, and buildings were constructed.
* {{ill|Shōhō|Q1146192|qid=Q1146192}} 3 (1646), 10th month – Shrine buildings were destroyed by fire.
* {{ill|Kanbun (era)|es|Kanbun|fa|کانبون (دوره)|fr|Ère Kanbun|id|Kanbun (era)|ja|寛文|ko|간분|ru|Камбун (нэнго)|simple|Kanbun (era)|sr|Канбун (ера)|sv|Kanbun|tr|Kanbun (dönem)|zh|寬文|qid=Q1146228}} 7 (1667) – By order of {{ill|Tokugawa Ietsuna|Q323422|qid=Q323422}}, {{ill|Kuze Hiroyuki|Q10859992|qid=Q10859992|lt=Kuze Yamato-no-kami Hiroyuki}} rebuilt the shrine buildings, which remain today. During the {{ill|Keiō|Q776775|qid=Q776775|lt=Keiō era}} (mid-19th century), the {{ill|cypress bark roof|Q90373477|qid=Q90373477}} roofing was changed to copper plate roofing.
* {{ill|Bunkyū|Q730266|qid=Q730266}} 1 (1861) – A commemorative match was held celebrating the succession of {{ill|Kondō Isami|Q467334|qid=Q467334}} as the fourth head of {{ill|Tennen Rishin-ryū|Q1445791|qid=Q1445791}}, later commander of the {{ill|Shinsengumi|ar|شينسينغومي|br|Shinsengumi|ca|Shinsengumi|de|Shinsengumi|es|Shinsengumi|fa|شینسنگومی|fi|Shinsengumi|fr|Shinsen gumi|he|שינסנגומי|hu|Sinszengumi|id|Shinsengumi|it|Shinsengumi|ja|新選組|ko|신선조|lt|Šinsengumi|ms|Shinsengumi|nl|Shinsengumi|pl|Shinsengumi|pt|Shinsengumi|ru|Синсэнгуми|simple|Shinsengumi|sq|Shinsengumi|sr|Шинсенгуми|sv|Shinsengumi|th|ชินเซ็งงูมิ|tr|Shinsengumi|uk|Сінсенґумі|vi|Shinsengumi|wuu|新选组|zh|新選組|zh_yue|新選組|qid=Q221031}}.

== Grounds ==
According to the saying of the enshrined deity, “pines bring sorrow—only cedars,” no pine trees are planted within the shrine grounds. As a result, in the local city of Fuchū, it is common to use “gate bamboo” instead of pine for New Year’s {{ill|Kadomatsu|ar|كادوماتسو|az|Kadomatsu|ca|Kadomatsu|de|Kadomatsu|es|Kadomatsu|eu|Kadomatsu|fa|کادوماتسو|fr|Kadomatsu|hu|Kadomacu|hy|Կադոմացու|id|Kadomatsu|ja|門松|jv|Kadomatsu|ko|카도마츠|mk|Кадомацу|ru|Кадомацу|th|คาโดมัตสึ|tr|Kadomatsu|uk|Кадомацу|vi|Kadomatsu|zh|门松|qid=Q2667233}}. The main sanctuary is built in the style of one structure with three sanctuaries, finished entirely in vermilion lacquer and roofed with copper plates. It was constructed in Kanbun 7 (1667) during the Edo period, changing from the earlier three-structure, three-sanctuary form to its current configuration. It is designated a cultural property of Tokyo Metropolis.  

The {{ill|Otabisho|Q11489117|qid=Q11489117}} is located at the “Fuchū City Hall Front” intersection ({{Coord|35|40|11.45|N|139|28|35.64|E|region:JP-13|name=Otobisho}}), and during the annual festival the portable shrines are carried there. Adjacent to it remains the takafuda notice board of {{ill|Fuchū-shuku|Q11486027|qid=Q11486027|lt=Fuchū-shuku}} (a Tokyo-designated cultural property). In addition, behind the Suijinsha within the grounds there is a place where the ritual of “hitogata nagashi” is performed, in which paper effigies are rubbed on the body and then floated down a river to cleanse impurity.<ref>[https://www.city.fuchu.tokyo.jp/kirari/sagasu/theme/jiman/ookunitamajinja_keidai.html Ōkunitama Shrine Grounds] Fuchū City official website (viewed January 21, 2018)</ref>  

Elsewhere on the grounds are a shrine office for amulets, waiting hall, kagura hall, treasure hall, {{ill|UNKNOWN|lt=temizuya}}, cloister, {{ill|UNKNOWN|lt=shamusho}}, {{ill|Wedding {{ill|Sumo|Q40561|qid=Q40561}} ring. Among these, the former Imperial Japanese Navy {{ill|Japanese cruiser Tama|de|Tama (Schiff)|fa|ناو تاما|fi|Tama (1920)|fr|Tama (croiseur)|id|Kapal penjelajah Jepang Tama|it|Tama (incrociatore)|ja|多摩 (軽巡洋艦)|jv|Prau dlajah Jepang Tama|sr|Јапанска лака крстарица Тама|sv|Tama (kryssare)|uk|Тама (крейсер)|vi|Tama (tàu tuần dương Nhật)|zh|多摩號輕巡洋艦|qid=Q1817205|lt=light cruiser Tama}} had Ōkunitama Shrine as its shipboard shrine; since October 25, 2014—70 years after its sinking—a memorial service has been held every year on the same date.<ref>[https://www.sankei.com/article/20171026-LBSXU2ML7ZLOFK36VSPEGHFQHA/ “May the cruiser Tama rest in peace: 100 attend memorial at Ōkunitama Shrine”] *Sankei Shimbun*, morning edition, October 26, 2017 (Tokyo)</ref>  

The entire precinct is non-smoking and bicycle riding is prohibited; however, during the {{ill|Cycling at the 2020 Summer Olympics|ca|Ciclisme als Jocs Olímpics d'Estiu de 2020|cs|Cyklistika na Letních olympijských hrách 2020|da|Cykling under sommer-OL 2020|de|Olympische Sommerspiele 2020/Radsport|es|Ciclismo en los Juegos Olímpicos de Tokio 2020|et|Jalgrattasport 2020. aasta suveolümpiamängudel|eu|Txirrindularitza 2020ko Udako Olinpiar Jokoetan|fa|دوچرخه‌سواری در المپیک تابستانی ۲۰۲۰|fi|Pyöräily kesäolympialaisissa 2020|fr|Cyclisme aux Jeux olympiques d'été de 2020|hu|Kerékpározás a 2020. évi nyári olimpiai játékokon|id|Balap sepeda pada Olimpiade Musim Panas 2020|it|Ciclismo ai Giochi della XXXII Olimpiade|ja|2020年東京オリンピックの自転車競技|ko|2020년 하계 올림픽 사이클|lt|Dviračių sportas 2020 m. vasaros olimpinėse žaidynėse|lv|Riteņbraukšana 2020. gada vasaras olimpiskajās spēlēs|ms|Lumba basikal di Sukan Olimpik Musim Panas 2020|nl|Wielersport op de Olympische Zomerspelen 2020|no|Sykling under Sommer-OL 2020|pl|Kolarstwo na Letnich Igrzyskach Olimpijskich 2020|pt|Ciclismo nos Jogos Olímpicos de Verão de 2020|ro|Ciclism la Jocurile Olimpice de vară din 2020|ru|Велоспорт на летних Олимпийских играх 2020|sv|Cykling vid olympiska sommarspelen 2020|th|กีฬาจักรยานในโอลิมปิกฤดูร้อน 2020|tr|2020 Yaz Olimpiyatları'nda bisiklet|uk|Велоспорт на літніх Олімпійських іграх 2020|zh|2020年夏季奧林匹克運動會自行車比賽|qid=Q39080749}}, the road race parade route passed through the grounds,<ref>[https://www.ookunitamajinja.or.jp/wp/info/2697.html Notice of traffic restrictions for Tokyo Olympics cycling road race (7/24–25)] Ōkunitama Shrine official website (viewed July 27, 2021)</ref> and many athletes rode their bicycles through the approach.

== Approach ==
The approach is lined with {{ill|Zelkova serrata|Q920344|qid=Q920344|lt=keyaki}}. This is said to date back to Minamoto no Yoriyoshi and Yoshiie, as well as Tokugawa Ieyasu. The “Keyaki Namiki Avenue,” officially known as the “Baba Daimon Zelkova Avenue,” stretches to the northern intersection before the Tokyo Metropolitan Agricultural High School and was designated Japan’s second natural monument in 1924—the only zelkova avenue so designated in the country.  

== Festivals ==
Nearly 400 rituals are held annually, including the daily offerings to the deities. Since 2018, the New Year’s bonfire rite {{ill|Sagichō Fire Festival|Q9332740|qid=Q9332740}} has newly been performed as a Shinto ceremony.

== Grand Festival (Kurayami Festival) ==
The grand festival of Ōkunitama Shrine is the {{ill|UNKNOWN|lt=Kurayami Festival}}, one of the three great unusual festivals of the Kantō region. Held annually from April 30 to May 6, it originally had the character of {{ill|Utagaki|Q610915|qid=Q610915}}, though its more licentious customs were reformed in the {{ill|Meiji era|Q3125096|qid=Q3125096}} era.
